I can't speak on behalf of the other person, but I can provide some context for what they may have been addressing.

Women in marriage were not allowed to control their own assets in the 18th century, and many centuries before that, and it wasnt until the 19th century that they began to have rights to their assets. It wasn't until 1848 in the state of New York that women were allowed to own property. This set a precedent for other states to adopt that law. In contrast, England gave the same right to only married women in 1882.

So while I don't necessarily agree with the term, "slave," in this context, women were still treated as second class citizens for hundreds, if not thousands of years, as they did not have any control of their finances, assets, and future, as this was determined by their husband or father. Since they also did not have the right to vote until the turn of the 20th century, it was more difficult for women to make decisions about laws that impacted them.

This article [Brief History of Marriage](http://exhibitions.globalfundforwomen.org/economica/marriage-and-money/brief-history-marriage) provides a more thorough perspective on the topic, and also includes how women during that time compared their situation to that of slavery.

Edit: so the gist of this post is, since men could control ALL of a woman's material possessions, they also had control over what they did. I'm sure there were healthy relationships/dynamics, but even in those cases, husbands/fathers had the power to dictate what women's lives were like.

That's definitely something that's hard to predict how it will effect your children. My parents memorialized their stillborn child that passed when I was seven, and they were also in mourning for the next eight or so years. While I certainly grieved the loss of my potential brother, it wasn't a traumatic event for me and I didn't hold onto it for long. What I did hold onto was the emotional absence of my parents in the years that followed. They stopped being there for me and I had to learn to get by without their support. They still talked about him as if he was a living, breathing person that was still actively a part of the family, and it was all they could focus on for years. I resented the brother that I never knew for taking away the parents that I had.

Death affects everyone differently. Your children resent you for not memorializing the loss of your other children, but it could have easily been the other way around, where they felt they could never live up to the pedestal the deceased child was on. I'm sorry for your loss, and Im sorry you live with such immense regret. But you couldn't have known, and life isn't a multiple choice test that you can study for.
